rows.title: Dragonfly for NestJS: a TypeScript backend with Sequelize — Migrations
rows.summary: `createTables = true` makes the tables at start, for development.
body: `createTables = true` makes the tables at start, for development. Once the database keeps data, leave it out and change
the schema with migrations in the project's `migrations/` folder:
dragonfly migrate make "notes on tasks"   # what the entities changed since the last migration
dragonfly migrate                         # applies the pending ones
dragonfly migrate down                    # reverts the last one
They are Sequelize migrations (`migrations/<time>_<name>.js` over `queryInterface`, `SequelizeMeta` in the database);
each one also keeps the schema it leaves, which the next `make` compares with. A renamed column shows as a drop and an add (`make` warns): edit the file into a rename to keep the data.

rows.title: Dragonfly for NestJS: a TypeScript backend with Sequelize — Relations, pages and transactions
rows.summary: Relations are TypeORM's decorators; the related entity is the field's type.
body: Relations are TypeORM's decorators; the related entity is the field's type. A relation field is optional: it is only
there when a query loads it, so no query is hidden.
`projectId` is the column of `project`: `Task(title = "paint", projectId = id)` puts a task in a project without
loading it. `@manyToMany(inverse = "tasks")` with `@joinTable()` on one side makes the join table (`tasks_tags`);
`@oneToOne` with `@joinColumn()` is the one-to-one. The compiler checks every rule (N0308).
`paginate` answers `Page<Task>`: `items`, `page` (from 1), `size`, `total`, `pages`. A use case whose writes must
happen together is `@transactional`: an `Err` (or an error) undoes them all.

body: dragonfly build                    # nuclear build .: writes build/ (src/, test/, package.json, tsconfig.json); compiles once installed
dragonfly install                  # npm install with the runtime (copied: build/.npmrc has install-links=true)
dragonfly run                      # npm run dev: http://localhost:3000 (PORT); restarts on every build (node --watch)
dragonfly test                     # npm test: the tests written in Nuclear
The same by hand, from `build/`: `npm install ~/.local/share/nuclearlang/packages/dragonfly-nest && npm install`,
`npm run dev`, `npm test`. While `dragonfly run` serves, `dragonfly build` (or saving a `.nuc` in VS Code) restarts the
server with the new code. ◉ Debug in VS Code (or F5 with `build/tasks_api.code-workspace`) runs the server under
the node debugger with its source maps: a breakpoint in a `.nuc` stops there.
`install-links=true` copies the runtime into `node_modules` (a link would make Node and TypeScript look for its
NestJS packages next to the runtime, not in the app). The generated `package.json` approves the install script of `sqlite3`, the driver of
the tests (npm 12 runs only approved scripts).

rows.title: Dragonfly for NestJS: a TypeScript backend with Sequelize
rows.summary: The `nestjs` dialect turns Nuclear into a NestJS 12 backend (ES modules): Sequelize repositories (`@nestjs/sequelize` + `sequelize-typescript`), DTOs validated with class-validator, Kafka events, Redis cache, and passes `tsc --strict`.
body: The `nestjs` dialect turns Nuclear into a **NestJS 12** backend (ES modules): **Sequelize** repositories
(`@nestjs/sequelize` + `sequelize-typescript`), DTOs validated with **class-validator**, Kafka events, Redis cache, and
**LangChain.js / LangGraph.js** tools, agents and graphs. The Nest modules are written for you. The generated code
passes `tsc --strict`. It uses the same kinds and query API as [Dragonfly for Python](python.md), so a project moves
between the two almost line by line.
This guide follows the example `examples/examples-backend/tasks_api`: a tasks CRUD, an event listener and an assistant
that reads and changes tasks. The full rules are in [nestjs.md](../../spec/nestjs.md).

rows.title: Dragonfly for Python: a backend with FastAPI and LangGraph — 4. Use cases, models and the API
rows.summary: Models of `domain/models/` are pydantic models with validation decorators (`@minLength`, `@max`, `@email`...).
body: Models of `domain/models/` are pydantic models with validation decorators (`@minLength`, `@max`, `@email`...). Use
cases hold the rules and answer a `Result`. A `controller` exposes them, NestJS style:
async def one(self, id: int) -> Result[AppError, Character]:
An `Err(NotFound(...))` becomes a 404, `Conflict` a 409, and an invalid body a 400, with no code in the controller.

rows.title: Dragonfly for Python: a backend with FastAPI and LangGraph
rows.summary: The `fastapi` dialect turns Nuclear into a Python 3.12+ backend: FastAPI endpoints, SQLAlchemy 2 async repositories, pydantic models, and LangChain / LangGraph tools, agents and graphs.
body: The `fastapi` dialect turns Nuclear into a Python 3.12+ backend: **FastAPI** endpoints, **SQLAlchemy 2 async**
repositories, **pydantic** models, and **LangChain / LangGraph** tools, agents and graphs. The generated code passes
`pyright --strict`. This guide walks through the example `examples/examples-fastapi/rick_api`: characters of a
show, a REST API and an agent that answers questions with a tool.
The full rules are in [fastapi.md](../../spec/fastapi.md) (the plain Python dialect: [python.md](https://github.com/nuclearlang/nuclear/blob/main/spec/python.md)).

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi`: the backend platform in Python
rows.summary: What this dialect adds to the platform's sheet: the project is generated as FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2 async + pydantic + LangGraph in `build/` (never edit it).
body: What this dialect adds to the platform's sheet: the project is generated as FastAPI + SQLAlchemy 2 async + pydantic +
LangGraph in `build/` (never edit it). `dragonfly build`, `dragonfly install` (a virtualenv), `dragonfly run`
(uvicorn), `dragonfly test` (pytest), `dragonfly migrate` (Alembic). Names are written in snake_case underneath; the
`.nuc` keeps camelCase and the compiler's messages use it. Full rules: `nuclear help fastapi`.

rows.title: Dialect `nestjs`: the backend platform in TypeScript
rows.summary: What this dialect adds to the platform's sheet: the project is generated as NestJS 12 (ES modules) + Sequelize + class-validator + LangChain.js in `build/` (never edit it).
body: What this dialect adds to the platform's sheet: the project is generated as NestJS 12 (ES modules) + Sequelize +

`dragonfly run` (node --watch), `dragonfly test` (node:test), `dragonfly migrate`. Full rules: `nuclear help nestjs`.

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi` (→ `fastapi`): the `backend` platform in Python — 1. Project
rows.summary: Generated once per project: `app/main.py` (the FastAPI `app`: config, component configs, controllers, listeners), `tests/conftest.py` (each test with the connections open, databases in memory) and `pyproject.toml`.
body: Generated once per project: `app/main.py` (the FastAPI `app`: config, component configs, controllers, listeners),
`tests/conftest.py` (each test with the connections open, databases in memory) and `pyproject.toml`.
**Architecture** (N0301, N0302): a use case is called only by its `appcomponent`; a repository by use cases,
aggregates and tools; a service by use cases and aggregates. Another component sees only the `appcomponent`,
models, entities, tools, agents, states and graphs.
**Libraries** (one per need, the most used): FastAPI (HTTP), pydantic (validation), SQLAlchemy 2 async with asyncpg /
`init_embeddings` (OpenAI and Ollama behind one API), LangGraph (graphs, checkpoints), Chroma (vectors). Their type
definitions come with the dialect: `nuclear defs search <text> --dialect fastapi`.

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi` (→ `fastapi`): the `backend` platform in Python — 2.1 Entity
rows.summary: TypeORM's decorators; the related entity is the field's type.
body: TypeORM's decorators; the related entity is the field's type. `@manyToOne x?: T` keeps its column in the field `xId`
(its own field, set without loading the row); `@oneToMany(inverse)` is the other side; `@manyToMany(inverse)` with
`@joinTable()` on one side makes the table `<table>_<field>` (columns `<entity>_id`); `@oneToOne` with `@joinColumn()`
on the side that keeps `xId`. `onDelete`: `"cascade"`, `"set null"`, `"restrict"`. A relation field is optional and
loaded only when a query asks for it (`relations("tasks")`); an unloaded one is absent from the JSON answer. N0308 when
a rule is not met. Setting a relation (`Task(projectId = id)`, `task.tags = [a, b]`) and saving writes it.
from dragonfly import Entity, Mapped, column, many_to_many, many_to_one, one_to_many, primary

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi` (→ `fastapi`): the `backend` platform in Python — 2.1 Entity
rows.summary: A table.
body: A table. In `components/<c>/data/entities/` the kind is given by the folder; elsewhere write `entity`. `@entity("table")` names the table (default: the name in snake_case). Each field is a column: `@primary(generated = true)` (a key the database gives: auto increment for an `int`, a uuid for a `string`), `@primary()` (a key the app gives), `@column(length = 100, unique = true, index = true, nullable = true, name = "x")`, `@created()`, `@updated()`; without a decorator it is a column too. Its SQL type comes from the field type; `name?: T` is nullable; a default goes to the column.
from dragonfly import Entity, Mapped, column, primary

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi` (→ `fastapi`): the `backend` platform in Python — 2.10 State and graph
rows.summary: A LangGraph `StateGraph`: `state` is its state, a pydantic model, so a node reads `state.field`; a field without a default gets its type's empty value (`""`, `0`, `[]`, `None` for `T?`), so a graph can start from a partial state; `messages: Messages` keeps a conversation.
body: A LangGraph `StateGraph`: `state` is its state, a pydantic model, so a node reads `state.field`; a field without a default gets its type's empty value (`""`, `0`, `[]`, `None` for `T?`), so a graph can start from a partial state; `messages: Messages` keeps a conversation. Each method of the `graph` is a node that receives the state and returns what changes; `@start` marks the first one and `@next("node")` the one after it (`"end"` ends). A node can also return `Command(goto = "node", update = {...})` to choose at run time. `~review.run(state, thread)` runs it.
from dragonfly.ai import Graph, next, start
async def ask(self, state: ReviewState) -> dict[str, str]:

rows.title: Dialect `fastapi` (→ `fastapi`): the `backend` platform in Python — 2.2 Repository
rows.summary: The data of one entity: `NameRepository` works on `Name` (or `@repository(Entity)`).
body: The data of one entity: `NameRepository` works on `Name` (or `@repository(Entity)`). It brings `find(id)` (`Ok(entity)` / `Err(NotFound)`), `findAll()`, `save(entity)` and `remove(id)`. Each method's lines build ONE query, created for that call (`q`): `where({...})` (equality, or `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `ne`, `like`, `ilike`, `oneOf`, `isNull`, `between`), `orderBy(field, desc = true)`, `limit(n)`, `offset(n)`, `relations("tasks", "tasks.tags")` (the relations to load); the last line runs it: `getOne()` (`Result`), `getMany()`, `paginate(page, size)` (`Page<T>`: `items`, `page` from 1, `size`, `total`, `pages`), `count()`, `exists()`, `update({...})`, `delete()`. The caller awaits it: `~characters.byName(name)`.

TypeORM's decorators; the related entity is the field's type. `@manyToOne x?: T` keeps its column in the field `xId`
(its own field, set without loading the row); `@oneToMany(inverse)` is the other side; `@manyToMany(inverse)` with

on the side that keeps `xId`. `onDelete`: `"cascade"`, `"set null"`, `"restrict"`. A relation field is optional and
loaded only when a query asks for it (`relations("tasks")`); an unloaded one is absent from the JSON answer. N0308 when
a rule is not met. Setting a relation (`Task(projectId = id)`, `task.tags = [a, b]`) and saving writes it.
